name: Rocky Mountain (Estes Park)
cover: Rocky Mountain National Park Bear Lake
tagline: Alpine tundra, elk meadows and the highest paved road in the US
summary: Estes Park is the mountain town at the door of Rocky Mountain National Park. Drive Trail Ridge Road above 12,000 feet, hike from Bear Lake to Dream and Emerald lakes, watch bugling elk in Moraine Park in autumn, and stay at the Stanley Hotel that inspired The Shining.
seasonNote: Trail Ridge Road opens late May to mid October; September brings golden aspens and the elk rut. Timed-entry permits are needed in summer.
arrival: Denver International is about 1 hour 45 minutes by car; shuttles run from the airport.
gettingAround: A car, plus the free park shuttle to Bear Lake in summer.
foodTip: Elk and bison burgers, Colorado craft beer and salt-water taffy.
buyTip: Taffy, outdoor gear and local art on Elkhorn Avenue.
baseArea: Downtown Estes Park or near the Beaver Meadows entrance

items.name: Trail Ridge Road
items.summary: Highest continuous paved road in the US, crossing tundra above 12,000 feet.
items.expect: Open late May to October; park entry fee.
items.tip: Stop at Forest Canyon Overlook and the Tundra Communities Trail.

items.name: Bear Lake to Emerald Lake
items.summary: Easy 3-mile round trip past Nymph and Dream lakes to Emerald Lake under Hallett Peak.
items.expect: Timed entry includes Bear Lake Road in summer.
items.tip: Start before 7 a.m. or take the shuttle.

items.name: Moraine Park
items.summary: Wide meadow where elk graze, with the Big Thompson River winding through.
items.tip: Dusk in September for bugling elk; keep your distance.

items.name: The Stanley Hotel
items.summary: 1909 hotel that inspired Stephen King's The Shining.

items.name: Sky Pond via The Loch
items.summary: Harder 9-mile hike past Alberta Falls and The Loch to a cirque lake.
items.tip: Start at dawn to beat storms.

items.name: Grand Lake
items.summary: Colorado's largest natural lake on the quieter west side of the park.
items.tip: Look for moose in the Kawuneeche Valley.

items.name: Elkhorn Avenue taffy and bakeries
items.summary: Main street of taffy pullers, fudge shops and cafés.
items.tip: Watch the taffy machines in the window.

items.name: Elk and bison burgers
items.summary: Local grills serving game burgers and Colorado beer.
items.tip: Ask for the elk sausage too.

items.name: Estes Park craft beer
items.summary: Brewpubs pouring Colorado ales after a hike.

name: Olympic (Port Angeles)
tagline: Rainforest, glaciers and wild coast in one park
summary: Port Angeles is the harbour town gateway to Olympic National Park, which packs three worlds together. Drive up to Hurricane Ridge for glacier views, walk the mossy Hall of Mosses in the Hoh Rain Forest, swim in Lake Crescent, and explore sea stacks and tide pools on Rialto and Ruby beaches.
seasonNote: July to September is driest; the coast and rainforest are wet most of the year.
arrival: Seattle–Tacoma International is about 2.5 hours by car and ferry; the Coho ferry links to Victoria, Canada.
gettingAround: A car is essential; the park has no internal roads linking its sides.
foodTip: Dungeness crab, smoked salmon and Pacific oysters.
buyTip: Lavender from nearby Sequim and local smoked fish.
baseArea: Port Angeles, Lake Crescent or Forks

connections.note: Drive with the Bainbridge or Kingston ferry.

items.name: Hurricane Ridge
items.summary: Mountain road to meadows with views of glaciated Mount Olympus.
items.expect: Park entry fee; check road status.

items.name: Hoh Rain Forest
items.summary: Temperate rainforest of moss-draped maples and giant spruce.
items.expect: Long drive; queues at the gate in summer.
items.tip: Walk the Hall of Mosses and Spruce Nature Trail.
items.why: One of the wettest places in the US.

items.name: Lake Crescent and Marymere Falls
items.summary: Glacial lake of clear blue water with an easy walk to a waterfall.
items.tip: Hike Mount Storm King for the view.

items.name: Sol Duc Falls
items.summary: Forest walk to a three-channel waterfall and hot springs resort.
items.tip: Soak in the hot springs after.

items.name: Rialto Beach and Hole-in-the-Wall
items.summary: Wild beach of driftwood and sea stacks with a sea arch at low tide.
items.tip: Walk to Hole-in-the-Wall at low tide.

items.name: Ruby Beach
items.summary: Sea stacks and tide pools at the park's most photographed beach.

items.name: Dungeness crab
items.summary: Sweet local crab steamed whole or in cakes.

items.name: Smoked salmon
items.summary: Pacific Northwest smoked salmon and chowder.

items.name: Port Angeles coffee and bakeries
items.summary: Cafés for an early start before the park.

name: Bryce Canyon
tagline: An amphitheatre of orange hoodoos under the darkest skies
summary: Bryce Canyon is a natural amphitheatre filled with thousands of orange rock spires called hoodoos. Watch sunrise from Sunrise and Sunset points, walk down among the hoodoos on the Navajo Loop and Queen's Garden trail, ride the rim to Rainbow Point, and stargaze in one of America's darkest skies.
seasonNote: May to October is best; snow on the hoodoos in winter is beautiful but cold.
arrival: Las Vegas is about 4 hours by car; Zion is 1.5 hours away.
gettingAround: A car, plus the free park shuttle in summer.
foodTip: Western steaks, Navajo tacos and fruit pie.
buyTip: Native American crafts and rock shop finds.

connections.note: Via scenic Highway 12 and Capitol Reef.

items.name: Sunrise and Sunset Points
items.summary: Rim viewpoints over the main amphitheatre of hoodoos.
items.tip: Be there at dawn; the light turns the hoodoos orange.

items.name: Navajo Loop and Queen's Garden
items.summary: 3-mile loop down through Wall Street's slot and among the hoodoos.
items.tip: Go down Queen's Garden, up Navajo.

items.name: Inspiration and Bryce Points
items.summary: Higher viewpoints taking in the whole amphitheatre.

items.name: Rainbow Point scenic drive
items.summary: 18-mile drive to the park's highest point with stops at Natural Bridge.
items.expect: Drive south first, stop on the way back.

items.name: Night sky programme
items.summary: Ranger astronomy talks and telescopes in a dark-sky park.

items.name: Red Canyon
items.summary: Red hoodoos and paved bike path on the drive in.

items.name: Kodachrome Basin State Park
items.summary: Colourful sand pipes and quiet trails.

items.name: Fruit pie in Tropic
items.summary: Small-town bakeries serving homemade fruit pie.

items.name: Western steakhouse dinner
items.summary: Cowboy steaks and buffets near the park entrance.

items.name: Navajo tacos
items.summary: Fry bread topped with chili, beans and cheese.

name: Sequoia and Kings Canyon (Three Rivers)
summary: Three Rivers is the gateway to Sequoia and Kings Canyon, home of the largest trees on the planet. Stand under the General Sherman Tree, climb the granite dome of Moro Rock, walk the Congress Trail through the Giant Forest, and drive into Kings Canyon, one of the deepest canyons in North America.
seasonNote: June to October is best; the Generals Highway can need chains in winter and Kings Canyon road closes November to May.
arrival: Fresno is about 1.5 hours away; Los Angeles and San Francisco are about 4 hours.
gettingAround: A car, plus the free Sequoia shuttle in summer.
foodTip: Californian diners, BBQ and farm stands in the foothills.
buyTip: Local art galleries in Three Rivers.
baseArea: Three Rivers or Wuksachi Lodge inside the park

items.name: General Sherman Tree
items.summary: The world's largest tree by volume, about 2,200 years old.
items.tip: Walk the Congress Trail loop after.

items.name: Moro Rock
items.summary: 350 steps up a granite dome to views of the Great Western Divide.

items.name: Giant Forest Museum and Big Trees Trail
items.summary: Easy loop around a meadow ringed by giant sequoias.

items.name: Crystal Cave
items.summary: Marble cave with polished formations.

items.name: General Grant Grove
items.summary: Grove holding the 'Nation's Christmas Tree'.

items.name: Kings Canyon Scenic Byway
items.summary: Drive down into a deep glacial canyon to Zumwalt Meadow and Roaring River Falls.

items.name: Three Rivers diners
items.summary: Roadside diners for big breakfasts before the park.
items.tip: Pack lunch, there are few options inside.

items.name: Foothills BBQ
items.summary: Smoked tri-tip, a Californian BBQ classic.

items.name: Wuksachi Lodge dining
items.summary: Restaurant inside the park among the forest.

name: Joshua Tree
tagline: Desert of twisted trees, giant boulders and starry skies
summary: Joshua Tree is where the Mojave and Colorado deserts meet, full of spiky Joshua trees and giant boulder piles. Scramble at Hidden Valley, watch sunset from Keys View, walk among glowing cacti at the Cholla Garden, and spend evenings in quirky desert towns like Pioneertown with its live-music saloon.
seasonNote: March to April for blooms, October to November for mild days; summer often tops 40°C.
arrival: Palm Springs airport is 1 hour; Los Angeles is about 2.5 hours.
gettingAround: A car; there is no shuttle or water in the park.
foodTip: Desert cafés, date shakes and roadhouse BBQ.
buyTip: Vintage shops and desert art in Joshua Tree town.
baseArea: Joshua Tree town, Yucca Valley or Twentynine Palms

items.name: Cholla Cactus Garden

items.name: Skull Rock and Arch Rock
items.summary: Boulders shaped like a skull and a natural arch.

items.name: Stargazing

items.name: Pioneertown
items.summary: 1940s Western movie set town turned quirky village.

items.summary: Domed wooden building offering sound baths.

items.name: Joshua Tree café breakfast
items.summary: Desert cafés serving big breakfasts before the park.

items.name: Date shakes

name: Death Valley
tagline: The hottest, lowest, driest place in North America
summary: Death Valley is a vast desert of salt flats, sculpted badlands and sand dunes. Stand at Badwater Basin, 86 metres below sea level, watch sunrise at Zabriskie Point, drive the pastel Artists Palette, walk the Mesquite Flat dunes and look down on it all from Dante's View.
seasonNote: November to March is mild; summer often passes 50°C and is dangerous for hiking.
arrival: Las Vegas is about 2 hours by car.
gettingAround: A car with plenty of fuel and water; distances are long.
buyTip: Date products and borax history souvenirs.

items.name: Badwater Basin
items.summary: Lowest point in North America, a white salt flat with hexagon patterns.
items.tip: Walk 1 km out to find clean salt polygons.

items.name: Zabriskie Point

items.name: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes
items.summary: Rolling dunes up to 30 metres tall.

items.name: Golden Canyon
items.summary: Hike through golden walls to the Red Cathedral.

items.name: Ubehebe Crater

name: Everglades (Homestead)
tagline: A river of grass with alligators and wading birds
summary: Homestead is the southern gateway to Everglades National Park, a vast wetland of sawgrass and mangroves. See alligators up close on the Anhinga Trail, cycle the Shark Valley loop, paddle mangrove tunnels, and stop at the famous Robert Is Here fruit stand on the way.
seasonNote: December to April is dry with more wildlife and fewer mosquitoes; summer is hot, wet and buggy.
gettingAround: A car; airboat tours run from the park's edges.
foodTip: Key lime pie, tropical fruit shakes and Cuban food.

items.name: Anhinga Trail
items.summary: Boardwalk where alligators, turtles and anhingas are almost guaranteed.
items.tip: Go in the morning in winter.

items.name: Shark Valley loop
items.summary: 15-mile paved loop by bike or tram to an observation tower.
